summary:
Montserrat is a British Overseas Territory and stands under the United Kingdom's framework, including compliance with international human rights instruments and the European Convention on Human Rights with its non-discrimination and equality obligations.

Same-sex sexual activity between consenting adults in private has been lawful in Montserrat since 2001. The change was made retrospectively by an Order in Council under sections 3(1) and 3(7) of the Caribbean Territories (Criminal Law) Order 2000, after the United Kingdom government concluded that the prohibitions violated international human rights agreements it had signed. Local politicians and religious leaders opposed the decriminalisation at the time. Sexual activity between women was never an offence.

Group sex and sex in public remain criminal offences for all persons. The age of consent is 18 for same-sex activity and 16 for heterosexual activity, so a visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship is held to a higher age threshold than a heterosexual visitor of the same age.

Article 16 of the Montserrat Constitution and Article 79 of the Labour Code prohibit discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation, with "discriminatory" defined as affording different treatment on grounds such as sex, sexual orientation, race, colour, language, religion or other status. Neither provision as cited names gender identity as a protected ground.

Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not legal in Montserrat. Article 10(1) of the Constitution protects only opposite-sex marriage, stating that every man and woman of marriageable age has the right to marry a person of the opposite sex and to found a family. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under local law has no route to have it recognised on the island.

Dedicated LGBTQ+ social infrastructure is close to absent. There are no gay bars, nightclubs or other venues on the island, although several hotels welcome gay tourists and operate non-discrimination policies. The island covers about 104 km2 and its resident base is small: the 1989 Hurricane Hugo and the 1995 Soufriere Hills eruption, which made the south uninhabitable and displaced more than half the population northward, left little density for community life.
tangentialFactors:
The 2001 decriminalisation was not initiated locally. It came from London through an Order in Council and was resisted by local politicians and religious leaders, who framed it as a cultural imposition by the United Kingdom. The legal position therefore rests on the United Kingdom's interpretation of its treaty obligations rather than on local political consensus.

The same action swept away the corresponding prohibitions in five United Kingdom territories in the region, including Turks and Caicos. The material reviewed covers only those territories and does not describe the legal position of neighbouring independent states in the region, so it cannot be assumed to extend beyond Montserrat.

Adherence to the European Convention on Human Rights is cited as the source of Montserrat's non-discrimination and equality obligations. The inventory records no case or complaint brought on that basis concerning Montserrat.
localsOnly:
For residents, protection against discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation is set out in Article 16 of the Constitution and Article 79 of the Labour Code.

Same-sex marriage and civil unions cannot be entered into locally, and Article 10(1) of the Constitution frames the right to marry as belonging to a man and a woman of marriageable age. No local process exists for legal recognition of a relationship read as same-sex.

The age of consent is 18 for same-sex activity and 16 for heterosexual activity, which affects residents between the ages of 16 and 18.

Decriminalisation in 2001 was carried through by an Order in Council based on the United Kingdom's treaty obligations, over the objections of local politicians and religious leaders.

There are no gay bars, nightclubs or other dedicated venues, though several hotels operate non-discrimination policies and welcome gay tourists.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no case law, tribunal decisions or complaints data showing how Article 16 of the Constitution or Article 79 of the Labour Code are enforced in practice, and no record of police conduct, charging practice or sentencing for group sex or public sex offences.

No source addresses gender identity as a protected characteristic, legal recognition of gender, or the process for changing gender markers on Montserrat documents; the same is true of entry and visa rules for trans travellers.

No sourcing was located on bathroom, changing-room or other facility access rules in Montserrat.

No hate-crime provision or trans-specific violence data for Montserrat was located in the sources reviewed.

The description of the island's social scene and the absence of venues comes from material dated 2012; current conditions are not independently confirmed by the sources reviewed.
